a3_landing: Four hundred steps down with lamps lit, and two landings on the way. The wall carvings start as proper mason's work and degrade below the first landing into gouges cut in a hurry by hands that were not holding dwarf tools. On the second landing there is a stair-shrine with nine niches cut into it at eye height.
a3_dark_descent: Four hundred steps in complete darkness with a hand on the wall, feeling the carvings change under the palm from tool-work into something scratched. At the ninetieth step something comes up past the company on the outer edge of the stair, entirely unhurried and breathing on a count of nine. It does not touch anybody as it goes by.
a3_scout_descent: The stair is roped and Kettle goes a full flight ahead of everybody, working on tugs: one for clear, two for wait where you are, three for come down after me. She gives one, and then another, and then a third, and then two in quick succession that mean nothing in the agreed code. After that the rope goes slack in your hands with no signal at all.
a3_shrine: The stair-shrine holds nine niches at eye height, eight of them containing dwarf tokens gone black with age and the ninth standing empty. The empty one is warm enough to feel from a foot away. The lip of the shrine below it has been worn into a groove by something set down there and taken back up a great many times.
a3_shrine_set: The relay iron goes into the warm niche, which accepts it the way a lock accepts its own key. The whole march goes quiet for the length of one breath. Then the count starts again somewhere below, slower than before and apparently satisfied, and it is no longer paying any attention at all to the stair.
a3_lit: A lamp struck on the stair catches the thing on the outside of the flight for exactly one second: a Warden's cloak, a Warden's boots, and above the collar nothing that a helmet would ever fit onto. It continues upward past the company without turning its head at all. Its count does not falter anywhere in the interval, before or after.
a3_overtake: The slack rope leads down two flights to Kettle, who is flat against the wall with her own hand over her mouth, alive and extremely angry about the necessity. She points down at the stairfoot. A Skree haulage gang is crossing the bottom of the stair in file with crates, and it is going to take some time.
a3_stairfoot: The foot of the relay stair is a crossing of ways in warm moving air. A flooded haulage gallery goes left with lamplight lying on the water; the deep pay-station stands ahead with its doors ajar; a chapel light burns to the right and a pump wheel turns somewhere below it. There is a breach into an old road-shrine, a cutting-shop with a cold forge, and at the far end of everything, a door.
a3_flood: The haulage gallery is chest-deep and as warm as bathwater, with lamplight further down it and a flat-bottomed barge poling toward you. Three Skree are aboard, working the pole in rotation. A crate is lashed amidships, eighteen inches of dwarf oak, and it is not making crate noises.
a3_flood_swim: Sixty yards of warm black water with kit held above the head, and the barge pole going past close enough to touch. Halfway across, something long turns over in the depth beneath the company, unhurried and entirely uninterested. It has the manner of an animal that has been extremely well fed on a schedule for a long time.
a3_ledge: The haulage ledge above the waterline is eleven inches wide, cut for maintenance rather than for men in mail carrying packs. The barge passes below close enough that you can hear the crate being spoken to. Whoever is speaking to it is using numbers, patiently, in the tone of somebody settling a child.
a3_ferry: Eleven seconds of violence in waist-deep water puts three Skree over the gunwale, and then there is nothing left to do but look at the crate. Eighteen inches of dwarf oak with air holes bored through the lid in a ring of nine. Inside it, something has stopped making noise in order to listen to you.
a3_crate: The crate holds a Warden of the Sixteen Mile garrison, alive, wrists bound in the Compact's knot and eyes bound in Reckoning linen. He is counting under his breath in the cadence Kettle set out with three cups and a knife on a table at Rell's Gate, and he is four numbers from the end of it.
a3_free: The lid comes off and the bound Warden is cut free and carried between two of you, dead weight and still counting steadily. Nyre holds his head as they go and tells him, over and over, that the number is wrong. It is the only argument anybody down here has, and he does not stop, and she does not either.
a3_gangpass: Three Skree lamps held at Skree height, and the company poles a haulage barge down a flooded dwarf gallery in the middle of a file that never once looks up. You learn the hours, the stations and the intervals in a quarter of an hour. You also learn what the crates are for, and how many of them there have been.
a3_payhall: The deep pay-station is ankle-deep and echoes badly. A rack on the far wall holds eight relay irons in eight sockets with a ninth socket standing empty, and the shift bell waits on its stand beside them. The road-paymaster lies face down across his own desk, and both of his sleeves are empty from the elbow.
a3_paymaster: Turned over, the paymaster has no hands and no other injury anywhere on his body. Inside his coat is a confession written by a man holding the pen in his teeth, which takes some time to read and longer to accept. He signed for four years, he says, because the alternative was explained to him carefully, and then he stopped signing.
a3_eight: Up close the rack is warm to the hand and every one of the eight irons sits in a socket warmer than the iron itself. The ninth socket stands empty and worn bright around the mouth. The whole rack is humming faintly, at the pitch a bowstring hums at in the moment before somebody loses their nerve.
a3_one_iron: One iron lifts out, and the rack's hum climbs a full tone as seven irons take up the load of the eighth's absence. Ilsabet says, quietly and with great precision, that the company now has about eleven minutes of the march's patience remaining. She then says that she is estimating, and that she would prefer nine.
a3_walltally: Behind the rack the wall carries a tally cut in groups of nine, going back nine hundred years in nine distinguishable hands and then further in a hand that is not dwarf work at all. In the final group eight strokes have been cut cleanly and evenly. A ninth has been begun and left at half its intended depth.
a3_chapel: The courier chapel holds nine benches and a wall of tally, and at a clerk's desk in front of them sits Ferrin Ostwyn, Reckoning priest, four months into the ninth hand's office. He stands up when the company comes in. He greets his sister by name before he greets anybody else, and he asks after their mother.
a3_terms3: Ferrin explains the arithmetic the way his order explains debt, which is to say completely and without apology. The thing behind the door cannot be killed and cannot wake while the count holds. Eight irons hold the lid, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the road has been paying that instalment since before the Reckoning existed to record it.
a3_offer: The offer is made plainly and without any threat in it. Ferrin is forty-one and will not survive another winter of the office, and it falls vacant on his death whether anybody has volunteered or not. For one of the five, named by the captain today, he will give up the iron, the road-book, the tower's arrears and nine more years of the road's peace.
a3_counter: The counter-offer is put to him straight: nine irons seated and no hand at all keeping any count afterwards. Ferrin's face does something complicated and entirely human. His order taught him that no debt simply ends, and he has spent four years proving the lesson, and he is not certain enough to refuse.
a3_attack: Ferrin does not defend himself and does not need to, because the chapel does it on his behalf. Nine benches worth of accumulated dust stands up in the approximate shapes of the people who once sat on them. Nyre's voice goes up for the first time since Gallowmere, and it is not addressed to the dust.
a3_kill_vale: Ferrin Ostwyn dies at his own desk in about the time it takes to say a number aloud, with his sister standing over him. The count stops everywhere in the march at once, which is not the same as stopping gradually. In the silence afterwards you can hear eight irons audibly taking up a load they were never meant to carry alone.
a3_valebook: Ferrin's tally-book and the ninth hand's ring come off a dead man's desk together. The book runs to eleven hundred pages in nine hands, and the last four months of it are in handwriting Nyre has known all her life. The ring is warm, and it is sized, unmistakably, for whichever hand lifts it next.
a3_wheel: The wheel-house under the pay-station holds a dwarf pump the size of a barn, its wheel turning steadily in a race of black water. Three of its nine paddles have been hacked away. A Skree crew is working on the fourth with axes, without any hurry at all, in the manner of people on a long and well-understood contract.
a3_pump: A short brutal fight in a very loud room, and then an hour of carpentry with Dellach and Vurma holding a paddle in place while Ilsabet lashes it. The water in the race drops a hand's width by the end of it. The lower march stays dry a while longer, for whatever that eventually turns out to be worth.
a3_flood_deep: The wheel jams on a pick haft and the race backs up within minutes, sending water the wrong way through nine hundred years of dwarf engineering. It goes down into the lower hall, where the crates are stacked in rows and the haulage file is still working. Nobody down there has been warned, and nobody up here can warn them.
a3_race: The wheel-race is crossed on the axle housing with the wheel turning a foot behind your head, nine paddles coming round in an order you can learn if you watch two full revolutions. The gap between two paddles is exactly as wide as one person who does not hesitate in the middle of it, and Vurma goes first.
a3_barrow: The breach in the march wall opens into a road-shrine the dwarves cut past and believed they had merely cut past. Nine road-wardens sit in stone around a tenth chair that is empty. Their plaques are still perfectly legible after nine centuries, and every one of the nine stone hands is pointing the same way.
a3_plaques: The nine plaques read in order, and they are not names at all but offices: the one who counts, the one who carries, the one who signs, and onward to the ninth, which is the one who is owed. All nine of the stone hands are pointing directly at the shrine's inner door. The tenth chair carries no plaque whatsoever, which Vurma says is considerably worse than a plaque would be.
a3_close: Two hours of rubble, mortar dust and Dellach's shoulder against a slab that does not want to move, and the breach is closed about as well as five people can close it. Everybody understands without discussing it that this is housekeeping rather than a solution. It will hold as long as nothing on the far side objects to being shut in.
a3_through: The way through the shrine's inner chamber to the door gallery passes nine empty stone chairs and one that is occupied. Whatever is sitting in it has been sitting there since before the dwarves cut the first gallery into this rock. It does not turn its head as the company files past, and it does not need to.
a3_forge: The cutting-shop is where the relay irons were made: a cold forge, a tally-die still bolted to its anvil, racks of blanks gone entirely to rust. The cutting-orders remain pinned to the bench under a stone weight. A dwarf smith is folded up beneath the bellows with his tools laid out beside him in careful order.
a3_cut: Three hours of cold work on a die that badly wants a striker and a proper smith, with Ilsabet reading the order stroke by stroke while Dellach swings and Vurma corrects them both. What comes off the anvil at the end of it is a ninth relay iron that is nine parts correct and one part entirely yours.
a3_die: The tally-die comes off the anvil in eleven minutes and wraps into forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what any relay iron says. Vurma calls it the only thing down here worth carrying out. Ilsabet calls it the only thing down here worth burying, and neither of them changes position on the walk to the door.
a3_orders: The cutting-orders read like any legion requisition until the final clause. Nine irons commissioned at the founding of the road, eight to be cut with the holding tally, and the ninth to be cut with a name left deliberately blank for the hand that would keep the count. The blank, the order notes twice, must never be cut a second time.
a3_hall: The door gallery is the last hundred yards and it is lit: nine niches, nine lamps, all trimmed within the hour. The air moves in and out along the floor on a nine-count that everybody has been hearing all day without naming. Halfway along, a pair of Warden's boots stands neatly against the wall with the tags still in them.
a3_door: The second door of the Compact stands at Hollowmarch under the mountains, dwarf iron set in a frame of much older stone, with nine sockets arranged in a ring. Eight of them are filled and warm and the ninth is empty and worn bright. The metal moves very slightly outward and back on a nine-count, and behind it, patient and enormous, is what the whole road has been feeding for nine hundred years.
e_a3_landing_rest: Twenty minutes on the first landing with boots off, which the schedule board warned about in chalk in words of one syllable. The stair's own traffic arrives on schedule and finds a company sitting down in the middle of a right of way that has been in continuous use for nine hundred years without a single interruption.
e_a3_shrine_take: A token comes out of the second niche, and the seven remaining tokens all turn a quarter turn in their sockets at the same moment. The stair below fills with the sound of somebody coming up two flights at a time. Whoever it is takes the corners without slowing down, which nothing on this road has done all week.
e_a3_count_steps: The steps are counted aloud in the dark to keep five people together, which works admirably as far as eight. At nine a second voice takes over the counting from somewhere below without any break in the rhythm. The company keeps descending, because the numbers keep arriving and every single one of them is correct.
e_a3_grab: A hand goes out to take hold of what is passing on the stair, and it turns out to be entirely willing to be held onto. It has been waiting a considerable time for somebody to initiate the transaction rather than merely submit to it. It is grateful in its own fashion, and it explains the arrangement at some length.
e_a3_slack: The rope is hauled in hand over hand and comes up cut clean at forty feet, with no scout and no signal on the end of it. The company climbs four hundred steps back up to a Warden tower in silence. There is a letter to be composed to a fen family about somebody who always went down first because she always went down first.
e_a3_shout: A hail goes down a dwarf hall in the correct Warden form and is answered accurately from six directions at once. The six voices belong to men the company heard reading a duty roster upstairs an hour ago, and all six get the form right. Every lamp out in the haulage gallery turns together toward the foot of the stair.
e_a3_sink: The barge is holed from underneath and goes down in eight feet of warm water with its crate still lashed amidships. The crate opens as it sinks, which is not something a lashed crate should be able to do. Whatever the Compact packed into it decides that the nearest hands in the water will serve perfectly well.
e_a3_swim: One breath taken, and one look down into warm black water with a lamp held under the surface to see by. The thing that has been turning over beneath the company for the whole crossing turns over once more, without any hurry at all, in order to look back up at the light and at what is holding it.
e_a3_ledge: The broken span of the ledge is taken as a shortcut, on the reasonable assumption that dwarf stone fails slowly and gives some warning first. It does fail slowly everywhere except here. Nine hundred years of warm water have been working patiently at the mortar from underneath, and they have finished the job this season.
e_a3_crate: The bound Warden is asked what he is counting toward, and he answers in detail, with dates and running totals, in a voice that becomes several voices before the end. Every lamp down the gallery stops its work in order to listen to the answer. The company is still standing in the water when it finishes, and it does not finish quickly.
e_a3_bell: The shift bell is rung once in a deep station, which is exactly what a shift bell is for. The garrison answers it: nine from behind the barracks barricade, the paymaster's clerks up out of the flooded gallery, and all of them forming into the old order to be paid what four years of arrears comes to.
e_a3_hands: A search for a dead paymaster's hands succeeds, which turns out to be the worst available outcome of the search. They are set in the wall's tally-groove, where they have been cutting the same nine strokes over and over for four years without supervision. They are still working when the lamp finds them, and they stop the moment they are noticed.
e_a3_eight_all: Eight relay irons come out of eight warm sockets in under a minute, taken by a company that came down here for a road-book and stayed for the arithmetic. The second door then does exactly what nine irons and nine hands were arranged to prevent. It has had nine hundred years to consider how it would like to do it.
e_a3_read_end: The wall-tally is read down to the bottom of the final group, where the ninth stroke has been begun and then abandoned at half its intended depth. Beside it a name has been cut into the stone in fresh, bright work that has not had time to dull at all. It is not the paymaster's name and it is not Ferrin's; it is the name of whoever happens to be reading it.
e_a3_burn_wall: A lamp breaks against nine hundred years of accounts and the chapel goes up in a light that shows exactly what is sitting on all nine benches. Ferrin stands in the middle of the fire entirely unharmed, apologising for the inconvenience to his sister specifically. Then he explains, patiently, that the tally has never once been kept on the wall.
e_a3_accept: A name is spoken aloud in a warm chapel and written into the book without hurry, and then blotted with care. The company walks out of the march four strong and genuinely rich, with the road safe for nine more years. That is a real thing that was really bought, and none of the four can look at it directly.
e_a3_accept_self: The captain's own name goes into the ninth hand's book, and the company is sent up the relay stair with the road-book, the iron and the tower's arrears. A new keeper sits down at a clerk's desk to learn a count that has been running since before this road was cut and shows no sign of concluding.
e_a3_hostage: Ferrin Ostwyn walks to the second door at knifepoint as surety, cooperative and entirely unsurprised. On the way he explains that a hostage is worth precisely what the other party is unwilling to lose. The thing behind this door has never been unwilling to lose anything, and he says he has watched it prove that four times.
e_a3_chapel_defends: A stand is made in a chapel against nine benches of standing dust, and the company wins it for something over ninety seconds. Then it loses, for the reason Ferrin did not think worth mentioning while there was still time to walk out. Everybody who has ever sat down in that room remains on the roll, and the roll is what is fighting.
e_a3_vale_count: The silence after Ferrin's death is waited out, to learn what a count does when it has no keeper at all. The answer arrives from the direction of the door inside four minutes. It looks for the nearest hand that has held an iron today, and it is not remotely particular about consent or about paperwork.
e_a3_wheel: A ride down the wheel-race on a paddle, to establish where the water actually goes. It goes to a shaft, and then to a sump, and then into a chamber that the dwarves pumped out continuously for nine hundred years for a reason that they wrote down in three separate places in three different languages.
e_a3_pump_stay: The company stays at the pump, because the lower march has to be kept dry and somebody has to keep it dry. Shifts are worked on dwarf machinery for eleven days. The door business is left for the Wardens, who arrive at the thaw and find a wheel in excellent order with nobody at all attending it.
e_a3_drown_own: The wheel jams on the captain's word with Kettle and Ossa still on the low side of the race. Nine hundred years of held water goes precisely where it has always wanted to go, considerably faster than anybody can climb a ladder. The shouting stops well before the water does, which is the part that stays with you.
e_a3_race: The wheel-race is crossed together and quickly, because the Skree crew has seen you and is shouting, which puts two people in the gap at the same moment. The gap between two paddles has always been exactly one person wide. The wheel does not adjust for enthusiasm, and it does not slow down for shouting either.
e_a3_ring: A ring is taken off the arm of a stone chair that has nobody sitting in it. All nine road-wardens turn their heads together to see who has accepted the office, which takes rather less time than stone should need. The plaque beneath the tenth chair turns out, on a second reading, to have been a job description.
e_a3_through: One long look at the occupied chair, taken deliberately, so that at least one person in the company would be able to say afterwards what was actually in the room. The thing in the chair returns the courtesy in full and at considerable length. By the end of it nobody is leaving to tell anybody anything.
e_a3_forge_light: A dwarf forge is lit for the first time in nine hundred years, because the company wants heat and working light and both are entirely reasonable requirements. The flue runs, as dwarf flues always do, straight up into the pay-station and straight down into the door gallery. It announces the work to everything that has ever worked here.
e_a3_second: A second ninth iron is cut on a die whose own written orders state, twice, that the blank must never be cut a second time. In the space of one hammer stroke the march's arithmetic acquires a tenth hand, for which it has no socket, no schedule, no precedent and no tolerance whatsoever.
e_a3_knock_door: Three knocks on the second door, since knocking worked so well at the gate at Sixteen Mile. The door answers them: three knocks returned from the other side in exactly the same rhythm, at a scale that brings dust off the ceiling and removes every opinion from everybody present in about two seconds.
e_a3_leave: Four hundred steps back up, out through the gate leaf, eleven miles of Lamp Road, and into Rell's Gate by the second evening. The report says the march is unsafe and says nothing else at all. Five people spend the rest of their lives not talking about the same afternoon, and two of them stop talking altogether.
e_a3_tags: Two Warden tags are lifted out of a pair of boots that were set down neatly by their owner in a place where nothing at all is neat by accident. The nine lamps of the gallery go out in order, from the far end. The boots turn out, on reflection, to have been a place setting rather than a memorial.
